questions.stem: What does collective pitch change on a helicopter rotor?
options: The pitch of all main-rotor blades together
Only the tail length
The number of rotor blades in flight
The direction of gravity
questions.explanation: Collective control changes the pitch of the main-rotor blades together and thereby changes rotor thrust.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of cyclic pitch control?
options: To make all blades stop rotating
To remove the need for a rotor
To change blade pitch around the rotor disc
To keep the aircraft mass constant
questions.explanation: Cyclic pitch varies with blade position and is used to tilt the rotor thrust direction.

questions.stem: Why can a powered single-rotor helicopter need an anti-torque system?
options: The cabin must rotate with the main rotor.
The rotor produces no aerodynamic drag.
The main rotor can operate only in a vacuum.
The driven main rotor applies a reaction torque to the airframe.
questions.explanation: Driving the main rotor produces an opposing reaction torque on the airframe; an anti-torque system can balance it.

questions.stem: How can a tail rotor help control a helicopter?
options: By changing the wing span
By producing a lateral force and yawing moment
By cancelling the weight of the engines
By stopping the main rotor in normal hover
questions.explanation: A controllable tail-rotor force can oppose main-rotor reaction torque and produce a yawing moment.

questions.stem: In forward flight, which blade generally sees the greater relative airspeed?
options: The blade advancing into the flight direction
The blade retreating from the flight direction
Both blades always see zero airspeed.
Neither blade moves relative to the air.
questions.explanation: Forward speed adds to rotational speed on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

questions.stem: What can limit helicopter speed on the retreating-blade side?
options: The absence of a rotor disc
The loss of all atmospheric pressure
A blade approaching aerodynamic stall
A compulsory change to a fixed wing
questions.explanation: The retreating blade can reach a high angle of attack and stall as forward speed rises.

questions.stem: What motion does a flapping hinge allow a rotor blade to make?
options: Only a change in blade material
Upward and downward motion relative to the rotor hub
A permanent increase in blade count
A complete stop in each revolution
questions.explanation: Flapping permits vertical blade motion and can help moderate differences in lift around the disc.

questions.stem: What is autorotation of a rotor?
options: A rotor that must always be driven by engine torque
A rotor locked to the fuselage
A rotor that can rotate by extracting energy from the airflow
A rotor that produces no aerodynamic force
questions.explanation: In autorotation, the airflow supplies energy to keep the rotor turning; it can be useful during a power-off descent.

questions.stem: What does the swashplate transmit to rotating rotor blades?
options: Cabin lighting commands only
Fuel directly into every blade
Landing-gear wheel speed
Pitch-control motion from the non-rotating airframe
questions.explanation: The swashplate transfers collective and cyclic pitch-control motion to the rotating blades.

questions.stem: What may be needed when rotor thrust is increased while keeping rotor speed?
options: More engine power
A complete loss of engine power
No change in rotor power under any conditions
A smaller number of blades immediately
questions.explanation: Increasing rotor thrust generally changes the power required; the engine must provide sufficient power to maintain rotor speed.
